o: We repeatedly delete every other element from a sorted list, alternating direction, until one number survives. For n = 9: left-to-right removes 1,3,5,7,9 leaving [2,4,6,8]; right-to-left removes 8 and 4 leaving [2,6]; left-to-right removes 2 leaving [6]. Since n can be up to 10^9, simulating the list is impossible — we need an O(log n) recurrence. The key observation is that after one full pass the problem reduces to the same game on n/2 elements with transformed values.
k: After one elimination pass on n elements, the remaining list is exactly the result of playing the same game on floor(n/2) elements, then mapping values back (either 2x or 2x-1 depending on parity of n).
The only extra state needed beyond n is the current direction; define f(n) as survivor for left-to-right start, then right-to-left is f'(n) = 2*(1 + n/2) - f(n) style mirror.

Recurrence: f(1)=1; f(n) = 2*f(n/2) if n even, else 2*f(n/2); but when n is odd or we go right-to-left, use f(n) = 2*(n/2 + 1 - f(n/2))... concretely f(n) = 2*(1 + n//2 - f(n//2)) handles both via mirroring.

a.i: Directly simulate the process: keep the list, remove every other element alternating direction until one remains. This mirrors the problem statement literally and is easy to reason about, but it costs O(n) time and memory per pass overall O(n), which fails for n up to 10^9 — it's included mainly to build intuition.
s: Repeat while len(arr) > 1: keep elements at odd indices (0-based) for a left-to-right pass, i.e. arr = arr[1::2]; for a right-to-left pass keep arr[::2] reversed appropriately.
a.t: O(n log n) time in total across passes (first pass is O(n), halving each time); actually O(n) sum — but memory O(n) makes it infeasible for n = 10^9.

a.i: Track three things instead of the whole list: the count of remaining elements, the first (head) value, and whether the next pass goes left-to-right. After each pass the count halves. The head changes to head + step whenever we eliminate from the left, OR when going right-to-left with an odd count (the first element gets removed). Otherwise the head stays. This yields an O(log n) loop with no recursion needed.
s: Initialize remaining = n, head = 1, step = 1, left = true.
While remaining > 1: if left, or (!left and remaining is odd), set head += step.
Halve: remaining /= 2, double step, flip direction.
a.t: O(log n) — the remaining count halves each iteration, so there are about log2(n) ≈ 30 iterations for n = 10^9.
a.sp: O(1) — only a few scalar variables.

w: In an interview, mention the simulation briefly to show understanding, then present the O(log n) head-tracking solution since n up to 10^9 rules out anything linear. Common pitfalls: forgetting that on a right-to-left pass with an odd count the head is also eliminated (only even counts spare the head); using int overflow in languages like Java/C++ when doubling step (use long internally). Edge cases: n = 1 returns 1 immediately; n = 2 returns 2. A likely follow-up: derive the closed-form / recursive formula f(n) = 2 * (1 + n/2 - f(n/2)) and prove it by symmetry between left-to-right and right-to-left games.
